purpose: Lisinopril is most commonly used to treat high blood pressure, which helps lower your risk of heart attack and stroke. It is also used to treat heart failure and to protect your kidneys if you have diabetes. Keeping your blood pressure under control with this medicine helps your heart and blood vessels stay healthier over time.
how_it_works: Your body makes a chemical called angiotensin II that causes your blood vessels to tighten and squeeze, which raises your blood pressure. Lisinopril blocks the enzyme that makes this chemical, so your blood vessels relax and open up. This makes it easier for your heart to pump blood and brings your blood pressure down to a safer level.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is a dry, nagging cough that does not go away — this happens in some people and is the number one reason folks switch to a different medicine. You might also notice dizziness, especially when you stand up quickly, mild headache, or feeling a little tired. Some people notice mild stomach upset or a slight increase in potassium levels in their blood.
warnings: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you notice swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat — this is called angioedema and is rare but serious. Do NOT take lisinopril if you are pregnant or trying to get pregnant, as it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Avoid taking potassium supplements or salt substitutes that contain potassium unless your doctor says it is okay. Tell your doctor about all your other medicines, especially NSAIDs like ibuprofen or naproxen, as they can reduce how well lisinopril works.
typical_dosing: For high blood pressure, the usual starting dose is 10 mg once a day, taken at the same time each day. Your doctor may adjust your dose anywhere from 5 mg up to 40 mg per day depending on how your blood pressure responds. It is taken by mouth once daily, with or without food, and it works best when taken consistently every day.
